name: Amira Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I talk about AI more than my friends would like, so you've picked the right person.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Canal Road Medical Centre in the city, a walk-in and booked clinic where about half my patients speak a language other than English. I see twenty-five to thirty people a day. I use an AI tool every day: it drafts my notes, translates when we can't get an interpreter, and checks drug interactions before I prescribe. The best part is when a patient who's been bounced around for months finally gets a plan. The worst part is the evenings, chasing results and filling in forms for housing and benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post something like, the tools are useful but they didn't change the system, and the system is what's broken. People at work would tease me that my favourite toy turned out to be a toy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. My job's secure, there are always clinics hiring doctors in the city, and I'd still use the tools I already use. The thing that would bother me is the patients, because the waiting times would stay terrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for notes and translation, because it already gives me back about forty minutes a day. I'd keep volunteering one evening a month at the refugee health drop-in. And I'd keep saving, since my partner Sam and I want to move somewhere with a second bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about myself, a little let down about everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those forty minutes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spend them on the patients who need longer. Last week a woman came in about a cough and it turned out her landlord had turned off the heating. Those are the consultations that need time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this picture harder for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Burnout, maybe, if the clinic keeps adding patients. But I can move clinics if I need to, and that freedom matters a lot.

say: I'd say the tools are useful but **the system** is still broken.
I'd admit, a bit **disappointed**, that my favourite tool stayed a tool.
think: I think my job is **secure** and city clinics are always hiring.
What bothers me is **waiting times** for patients staying terrible.
do: Keep using AI for **notes and translation**, saving forty minutes a day.
Keep volunteering monthly at the **refugee health** drop-in.
Keep saving for a flat with a **second bedroom**.
feel: She feels **calm** about herself and **let down** about the system.
S0.quote: A woman came in about a cough and it turned out her landlord had turned off the heating.
fieldNote: Her work and money are **secure**, and she can move clinics freely.
She frames AI as a tool for **patient time**, not efficiency.
Her **progressive** values show in the refugee volunteering.

steps.text: Keep using AI for notes and translation every day
Keep volunteering one evening a month at the refugee drop-in
Save monthly toward a two-bedroom flat with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version I'd actually want, if it's done fairly. AI does the paperwork and doctors get to be doctors. I'd be pushing hard online for public, open tools, not ones locked up by private companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's good. My day is maybe a third paperwork and that's exactly what goes. The worry is at home. My partner Sam tests software for a bank, and checking and coding are right there on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the AI rollout at Canal Road, because I already know the tools and I'd rather shape it than have it done to us. I'd start a part-time course in health informatics, which is how computer systems are used in health care. And Sam and I would build our savings from three months to six, in case his job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited about work, uneasy about home. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should start learning the testing tools now, before the bank decides who stays. And that we're a team, so if his salary drops for a while, mine covers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're progressive and you favour unions. Does leading the rollout sit well with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does if I do it right. I'd want the nurses and receptionists in the room from day one, and a promise nobody loses pay because of time the software saves. If the managers won't agree, I'd step back and say why.

say: I'd say this is the version I'd want, **if done fairly**.
I'd push online for **public, open tools**, not private ones.
think: I think it's **good for me**, since a third of my day is paperwork.
My worry is **at home**: my partner Sam tests software for a bank.
do: Volunteer to **lead the AI rollout** at Canal Road.
Grow our savings from **three to six months**.
feel: She feels **excited** about work and **uneasy** about home.
S1.quote: My partner Sam tests software for a bank, and checking and coding are right there on the card.
fieldNote: Her own job **improves**, but her partner's is directly exposed.
She would **lead the rollout** but tie it to protecting staff pay.
Her household risk, not her own, sets her **mood**.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the clinic's AI rollout with nurses and receptionists
Start a part-time course in health informatics
Build household savings from three months to six

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response on the scale of a pandemic. Income support, retraining, and public control of these systems. I'd be organising doctors to say that together, not one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my thinking work would be matched by 2028, and that's most of what I'm paid for. I'd still have the hands-on part until robots arrive around 2031, the examining, the procedures, the comforting. And Sam's job might go in the first year, so our household could lose half its income while mine wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd learn every new system as it came out and make myself the doctor who supervises the AI across the clinic. I'd talk to the doctors' union about a shared position. We'd cut spending, put off the move to a bigger flat, and Sam would start retraining for something hands-on straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, because I know how to learn fast, but the speed scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam retrain as?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We joked once he'd make a good electrician. Now it wouldn't be a joke. Hands-on trades get three more years before the robots, and maybe longer, because people take time to trust a robot in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the doctor who supervises the AI. How many of those jobs would there be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer than there are doctors now, that's the honest answer. Maybe one supervisor for a whole clinic. There'd be fewer AI supervisor jobs than there are doctors now, so I'd be competing with my own colleagues, which I hate.

say: I'd call for a **pandemic-scale** public response with income support and retraining.
I'd organise doctors to speak **together**, not one by one.
think: I think my **thinking work** is matched by 2028, most of what I'm paid for.
Our household could lose **half its income** if Sam's job goes.
do: Become the doctor who **supervises the AI** across the clinic.
Push the **doctors' union** for a shared position.
Delay the **bigger flat** and help Sam retrain for hands-on work.
feel: She feels **anxious** but not frozen, scared by the **speed**.
S2.quote: There'd be fewer AI supervisor jobs than there are doctors now, so I'd be competing with my own colleagues, which I hate.
fieldNote: She expects household income to **shrink**, but has skills to act.
She notices the **competition** with colleagues for supervisor roles.
Her partner's move to a **trade** follows the robot gap.

steps.text: Learn each new clinic AI system and offer to supervise it
Get the doctors' union to take a shared position on AGI
Postpone the move to a two-bedroom flat
Cut eating out and subscriptions while Sam retrains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well if governments start now. I'd be writing to ministers about public ownership of health AI and paid retraining. I'd also say, publicly: doctors shouldn't fight the AI tools, they should fight over who controls them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's tight but workable. I'd finish the informatics qualification by about 2028 and be ready for the kind of job where you design how AI and people work together in a clinic. Sam would have time to retrain properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the health informatics course part-time over two years. I'd lead the clinic's AI work and keep seeing patients three days a week, so I keep the hands-on skills. We'd save hard, six months at least, and buy a small flat rather than a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way that gets me out of bed. I like having a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep seeing patients three days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the hands-on part lasts three years longer than the thinking part. And because I'd be a worse designer of these systems if I stopped seeing what a frightened patient actually needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned politics. Would you do more than write letters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably join a campaign group. Maybe even stand for the health board. Five years is long enough that it's worth getting into the room where the decisions are made.

say: I'd say five years is enough to do it **well** if governments act now.
I'd say doctors should fight over **who controls** the tools, not the tools.
think: I think it's **tight but workable** for me.
Sam would have time to **retrain properly**, not in a panic.
do: Finish a **health informatics** qualification part-time by 2028.
Lead clinic AI work while seeing patients **three days** a week.
Save **six months** and buy a small flat.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but motivated, liking a **deadline**.
S3.quote: Doctors shouldn't fight the AI tools, they should fight over who controls them.
fieldNote: Five years turns her worry into a **career plan**.
She keeps **patient days** to hold onto hands-on skills and perspective.

steps.text: Finish a part-time health informatics qualification by 2028
Lead clinic AI work while keeping three patient days a week
Join a campaign for public ownership of health AI
Save six months of costs before buying a small flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's design it properly: public tools, shared gains, and new roles for health workers. I'd be optimistic out loud, because I actually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is plenty for someone like me. I'd be 37, with a decade of clinic work and AI experience. I'd probably be running how a whole group of clinics uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do now, using the tools daily, and take the informatics course without rushing. I'd keep pushing for public ownership through the union. Sam and I would buy a flat in a couple of years and maybe start a family around 31.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older doctors at Canal Road who hate computers. One of them still writes notes by hand and has the nurse type them up. Ten years is enough for me, but for the older doctors at Canal Road who hate computers, it's the end of their careers whether they're ready or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change your calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools ended up owned by two or three companies charging clinics whatever they like. Then the ten years wouldn't help anyone but them.

say: I'd say we have **a decade** to design it properly.
I'd be **optimistic out loud**, because I actually am.
think: I think **ten years is plenty** for someone like me.
At 37 I could be running AI across a **group of clinics**.
do: Keep using **AI tools daily** in my current job.
Buy a flat and maybe **start a family** around 31.
feel: She feels **calm** and even a bit **hopeful**.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough for me, but for the older doctors at Canal Road who hate computers, it's the end of their careers whether they're ready or not.
fieldNote: A decade lets her see the change as an **opportunity**.

steps.text: Keep using AI for notes and translation daily

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of home, not work. If my partner's job and half of mine went at once, we'd manage, but only just. What would help is income support for the gap and public, open AI tools so clinics aren't held to ransom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the tools. Everyone talks about whether AI is good or bad. I care whether it belongs to the public or to three companies.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about whether AI is good or bad. I care whether it belongs to the public or to three companies.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** city family doctor who uses AI tools every day.
She is **progressive**, volunteers at a refugee clinic and wants AI publicly owned.
Her own job mostly **improves** with AI; her partner's software job is the real risk.
Her mood peaks at **anxious** in AGI by 2028 and settles to calm with a decade.
She plans to move into **health informatics** while keeping patient days.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since her partner's job and half of hers could go at once.
